solution_overview:
Nine distinct musicians must sit in a single row of nine chairs. There are three violinists, three cellists, two flutists, and one pianist. Every seating arrangement of the nine people is equally likely. We model this as permutations of distinct items.

First, we establish the total number of possible arrangements by permuting the nine distinct musicians. This total will serve as the denominator for all probability calculations.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The total number of ways to arrange $n$ distinct items in a row is given by $n!$.

$$N_{\text{total}} = 9!$$

$$N_{\text{total}} = 362,880$$

This matches the number given in the statement, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

To find the probability that three specific people (the violinists) sit in three consecutive chairs, we can treat the block of three violinists as a single unit. We then arrange this unit and the remaining $n-3$ musicians, and multiply by the number of ways the violinists can arrange themselves within their block.

$$P(\text{all three violinists together}) = \frac{(n-3+1)! \times 3!}{n!}$$

Here, $n=9$ musicians total. The three violinists form a block, so we arrange $9-3=6$ other musicians plus the block, making $6+1=7$ items to arrange. The three violinists can arrange themselves in $3!$ ways within their block.

$$P(\text{all three violinists together}) = \frac{7! \times 3!}{9!}$$

$$P(\text{all three violinists together}) = \frac{5040 \times 6}{362880}$$

$$P(\text{all three violinists together}) = \frac{30240}{362880} = \frac{1}{12}$$

The calculated probability is exactly $1/12$, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

To find the probability that the two flutists sit adjacent to each other, we treat the pair of flutists as a single unit. We then arrange this unit and the remaining $n-2$ musicians, and multiply by the number of ways the flutists can arrange themselves within their block.

$$P(\text{two flutists together}) = \frac{(n-2+1)! \times 2!}{n!}$$

With $n=9$ musicians, the two flutists form a block. We arrange $9-2=7$ other musicians plus the block, making $7+1=8$ items to arrange. The two flutists can arrange themselves in $2!$ ways within their block.

$$P(\text{two flutists together}) = \frac{8! \times 2!}{9!}$$

$$P(\text{two flutists together}) = \frac{8! \times 2 \times 1}{9 \times 8!} = \frac{2}{9}$$

$$P(\text{two flutists together}) \approx 0.2222 \approx 22.22\%$$

Since $22.22\%$ is not greater than $25\%$, the statement is False.

**D.** → True

To find the probability that a specific musician (the pianist) sits in one of the two end chairs, we can count the favorable arrangements and divide by the total possible arrangements. There are two end chairs the pianist can occupy.

$$P(\text{pianist in an end chair}) = \frac{\text{Number of favorable arrangements}}{\text{Total number of arrangements}}$$

If the pianist is in one of the two end chairs, there are $2$ choices for their position. The remaining $9-1=8$ musicians can be arranged in the remaining $8$ chairs in $8!$ ways.

$$P(\text{pianist in an end chair}) = \frac{2 \times 8!}{9!}$$

$$P(\text{pianist in an end chair}) = \frac{2 \times 8!}{9 \times 8!} = \frac{2}{9}$$

This probability is exactly $2/9$, so the statement is True.

**E.** → True

To find the probability that the three violinists sit together as a block AND the three cellists sit together as a block, we treat each group as a single unit. We arrange these two units and the remaining musicians, then multiply by the internal arrangements within each block.

$$P(\text{violinists together AND cellists together}) = \frac{\text{Number of favorable arrangements}}{\text{Total number of arrangements}}$$

The three violinists form one block ($3!$ internal arrangements) and the three cellists form another block ($3!$ internal arrangements). The remaining musicians are two flutists and one pianist, totaling $3$ individuals. So we are arranging $1$ (violin block) $+ 1$ (cellist block) $+ 3$ (other individuals) $= 5$ items. These $5$ items can be arranged in $5!$ ways.

$$P(\text{violinists together AND cellists together}) = \frac{5! \times 3! \times 3!}{9!}$$

$$P(\text{violinists together AND cellists together}) = \frac{120 \times 6 \times 6}{362880}$$

$$P(\text{violinists together AND cellists together}) = \frac{4320}{362880} = \frac{1}{84}$$

$$P(\text{violinists together AND cellists together}) \approx 0.0119 \approx 1.19\%$$

Since $1.19\%$ is less than $2\%$, the statement is True.
